Experiments in language evolution: inferences from closed- vs open-ended semantic space paradigms

Data modeling

analysis by Aleksandra Ćwiek

24 November, 2025

1 What this document does

Purpose. This notebook fits and evaluates baseline hierarchical models for three outcome measures that capture how well participants’ free-text responses match target concepts:

  1. binary_guess — whether the response was judged exact/near-exact (yes/no),

  2. judged_similarity — coder-assigned similarity on a four-point scale,

  3. cosine_rescaled — automatic cosine similarity (ConceptNet, rescaled to [0,1]).

Each outcome is analyzed separately. We summarize posterior distributions, report Bayesian R², and check convergence/diagnostics.

Inputs. One cleaned, analysis-ready dataset from 1_preparation.Rmd (data/final_df.csv), containing participant IDs, stimulus/concept IDs, language, and the three outcome measures.

Outputs.

  • Cached fitted models in models/ (RDS files).

  • Summary tables (posterior means/HDIs, random-effect SDs, Bayesian R²).

  • Diagnostic plots and posterior predictive checks.

  • Figures saved to plots/2_modeling/ (auto-saved with stable numbering).

# --- plot hook to auto-save ---
.default_plot_hook <- knitr::knit_hooks$get("plot")
.has_magick <- requireNamespace("magick", quietly = TRUE)

knitr::knit_hooks$set(plot = function(x, options){
  res <- if (is.function(.default_plot_hook)) .default_plot_hook(x, options) else NULL

  if (!is.null(options$fig.cap)) {
    fig_no <- get(".last_fig_no", envir = .GlobalEnv, inherits = FALSE)
    if (!is.na(fig_no)) {
      fig_no_str <- sprintf("%02d", fig_no)

      # subfolder = Rmd filename without extension
      rmd_name <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(knitr::current_input()))
      target_dir <- file.path(plots, rmd_name)
      if (!dir.exists(target_dir)) dir.create(target_dir, recursive = TRUE)

      png_out <- file.path(target_dir, paste0("Figure_", fig_no_str, ".png"))
      tif_out <- file.path(target_dir, paste0("Figure_", fig_no_str, ".tif"))

      file.copy(x, png_out, overwrite = TRUE)

      if (.has_magick) {
        img <- magick::image_read(png_out)
        magick::image_write(img, path = tif_out, format = "tiff", compression = "lzw")
      } else {
        file.copy(png_out, tif_out, overwrite = TRUE)
      }
    }
  }

  res
})

Other helpers

bb_corr <- function(x, y, R = 4000, seed = 1708) {
  stopifnot(length(x) == length(y))
  set.seed(seed)
  n <- length(x)
  out <- numeric(R)
  for (r in seq_len(R)) {
    w <- rexp(n)          # Dirichlet via i.i.d. Exponential then normalize
    w <- w / sum(w)
    mx <- sum(w * x); my <- sum(w * y)
    sx <- sqrt(sum(w * (x - mx)^2))
    sy <- sqrt(sum(w * (y - my)^2))
    out[r] <- sum(w * (x - mx) * (y - my)) / (sx * sy)
  }
  out
}

summ_post <- function(draws, name){
  h <- hdi(draws, ci = 0.95)
  tibble(pair = name,
         mean = mean(draws),
         median = median(draws),
         hdi_low = h$CI_low,
         hdi_high = h$CI_high)
}

bf_bic <- function(y, x){
  fit1 <- lm(y ~ x)
  fit0 <- lm(y ~ 1)
  BIC0 <- BIC(fit0); BIC1 <- BIC(fit1)
  # BF10 ≈ exp((BIC0 - BIC1)/2)
  exp((BIC0 - BIC1)/2)
}

4 Modeling

4.1 What we model

  • Binary accuracy: binary_guess ∈ {0,1}, modeled with a Bernoulli distribution and logit link.

  • Ordinal judgments: judged_similarity ∈ {0,1,2,3}, modeled with a cumulative logit (ordinal) likelihood.

  • Cosine similarity: cosine_rescaled ∈ [0,1], modeled with a zero-one-inflated Beta (ZOIB) or a simpler Beta after applying an ε-open transform to handle boundary values.

All models include varying intercepts for participants and stimuli to account for individual and item-level heterogeneity.

4.2 Full (for Cognitive Science)

We fit baseline models for each of the three measures, with only random intercepts for participant, native language, and stimulus.

{
  set.seed(1708)

  ## ---- ensure models dir exists (you already have `models` as an absolute path) ----
  if (!dir.exists(models)) dir.create(models, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

  ## ---- data prep (minimal; no z-scoring of cosine) ----
  ## ---------- COMPLETE-CASE DATA (based on cosine)
  # Rationale: use the same rows for all three outcomes to enable direct comparability
  if (!"ord_norm" %in% names(df)) df$ord_norm <- df$judged_similarity / 3
  df_brm <- subset(df, !is.na(cosine_rescaled))

  ## Keep exact-1 spike info for reporting (from original column but CC rows)
  ones_table_stim <- aggregate(I(df_brm$cosine_rescaled == 1) ~ stimulus_concept, data = df_brm, FUN = mean)
  names(ones_table_stim) <- c("stimulus_concept", "one_rate")

  df_brm$participant      <- factor(df_brm$participant)
  df_brm$stimulus_concept <- factor(df_brm$stimulus_concept)
  df_brm$native_language  <- factor(df_brm$native_language) # decided to do without it because it was not variable and caused much longer computation times
  df_brm$judged_ord       <- factor(df_brm$judged_similarity, levels = 0:3, ordered = TRUE)
 # Replace values extremely close to 1 with exactly 1
  df_brm$cosine_rescaled <- ifelse(
    !is.na(df_brm$cosine_rescaled) & df_brm$cosine_rescaled > 1 & df_brm$cosine_rescaled <
      1.001,
    1,
    df_brm$cosine_rescaled
  )
  
  ## ---- cosine preparation (rescaling to make comparable across measures) ----
  
  rescale_to_unit <- function(x) {
    eps <- 1e-10
    tiny <- 1e-12
    
    # Step 1: Epsilon-open to avoid exact boundaries
    x_open <- pmin(pmax(x - eps, tiny), 1 - tiny)
    
    # Step 2: Min-max rescale to [0,1]
    xmin <- min(x_open, na.rm = TRUE)
    xmax <- max(x_open, na.rm = TRUE)
    span <- xmax - xmin
    
    if (!is.finite(span) || span <= 0) {
      stop("Cannot rescale: no variation in x")
    }
    
    x_scaled <- (x_open - xmin) / span
    
    # Step 3: Ensure strictly in (0,1) for Beta
    x_final <- pmin(pmax(x_scaled, tiny), 1 - tiny)
    
    return(x_final)
  }
  
  # Apply to data
  # Nudge exact 1.0s only (keeping original scale)
  df_brm$cosine_original <- df_brm$cosine_rescaled
  df_brm$cosine_original[df_brm$cosine_original == 1.0] <- 0.999999
  
  # Full min-max rescaling (for comparable plot)
  df_brm$cosine_scaled <- rescale_to_unit(df_brm$cosine_rescaled)
  
  ## ---- very wide priors for baselines / couplings (not for ZOIB components) ----
  .pri_bin <- c(
    set_prior("normal(0, 5)", class = "Intercept"),
    #set_prior("normal(0, 2)", class = "b"),
    set_prior("student_t(3, 0, 5)", class = "sd")
  )
  .pri_ord <- c(
    set_prior("normal(0, 5)", class = "Intercept"),  # thresholds
    #set_prior("normal(0, 2)", class = "b"),
    set_prior("student_t(3, 0, 5)", class = "sd")
  )
  .pri_wide <- c(
    set_prior("normal(0, 5)", class = "Intercept"),
    #set_prior("normal(0, 2)", class = "b"),
    set_prior("student_t(3, 0, 5)", class = "sd")
  )

  ## ========================= BASELINES =========================
  .bin_rds <- file.path(models, "fit_bin.rds")
  if (file.exists(.bin_rds)) {
    fit_bin <- readRDS(.bin_rds)
  } else {
    fit_bin <- brm(
      binary_guess ~ 1 + (1|p|participant) + (1|s|stimulus_concept),
      data    = df_brm,
      family  = bernoulli(),
      prior   = .pri_bin,
      backend = "cmdstanr",
      chains  = 4, iter = 8000, warmup = 4000, 
      threads = threading(2), cores = parallel::detectCores(),
      control = list(adapt_delta = 0.97, max_treedepth = 12),
      seed    = 1708, refresh = 100,
      save_pars = save_pars(all = TRUE)
    )
    saveRDS(fit_bin, .bin_rds)
  }

  .ord_rds <- file.path(models, "fit_ord.rds")
  if (file.exists(.ord_rds)) {
    fit_ord <- readRDS(.ord_rds)
  } else {
    fit_ord <- brm(
      judged_ord ~ 1 + (1|p|participant) + (1|s|stimulus_concept),
      data    = df_brm,
      family  = cumulative(link = "logit"),
      prior   = .pri_ord,
      backend = "cmdstanr",
      chains  = 4, iter = 10000, warmup = 4000, 
      threads = threading(2), cores = parallel::detectCores(),
      control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99, max_treedepth = 13),
      seed    = 1708, refresh = 100,
      save_pars = save_pars(all = TRUE)
    )
    saveRDS(fit_ord, .ord_rds)
  }

  .cos_org_rds <- file.path(models, "fit_cos_org.rds")
  if (file.exists(.cos_org_rds)) {
    fit_cos_org <- readRDS(.cos_org_rds)
  } else {
    fit_cos_org <- brm(
      cosine_original ~ 1 + (1|p|participant) + (1|s|stimulus_concept),
      data    = df_brm,
      family  = Beta(), 
      prior = c(
        set_prior("normal(0, 2)", class = "Intercept"),
        set_prior("student_t(3, 0, 2.5)", class = "sd"),
        set_prior("gamma(0.01, 0.01)", class = "phi")),
      backend = "cmdstanr",
      chains  = 4, iter = 10000, warmup = 4000, 
      threads = threading(2), cores = parallel::detectCores(),
      control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99, max_treedepth = 13),
      seed    = 1708, refresh = 100,
      save_pars = save_pars(all = TRUE)
    )
    saveRDS(fit_cos_org, .cos_org_rds)
  }
  
  .cos_com_rds <- file.path(models, "fit_cos_com.rds")
  if (file.exists(.cos_com_rds)) {
    fit_cos_com <- readRDS(.cos_com_rds)
  } else {
    fit_cos_com <- brm(
      cosine_scaled ~ 1 + (1|p|participant) + (1|s|stimulus_concept),
      data    = df_brm,
      family  = Beta(), 
      prior = c(
        set_prior("normal(0, 2)", class = "Intercept"),
        set_prior("student_t(3, 0, 2.5)", class = "sd"),
        set_prior("gamma(0.01, 0.01)", class = "phi")),
      backend = "cmdstanr",
      chains  = 4, iter = 10000, warmup = 4000, 
      threads = threading(2), cores = parallel::detectCores(),
      control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99, max_treedepth = 13),
      seed    = 1708, refresh = 100,
      save_pars = save_pars(all = TRUE)
    )
    saveRDS(fit_cos_com, .cos_com_rds)
  }

  ## ---- compact Bayes R^2 (kept as r2_table) ----
  # Path to saved R2 summary
  .r2_rds <- file.path(models, "r2_table.rds")
  
  if (file.exists(.r2_rds)) {
    # If the summary table already exists, just load it
    r2_table <- readRDS(.r2_rds)
    message("Loaded existing r2_table from ", .r2_rds)
  
  } else {
    # Otherwise, compute it fresh from model fits
    .r2 <- function(fit) {
      r <- bayes_R2(fit)
      c(Estimate = mean(r),
        Q2.5 = quantile(r, .025),
        Q97.5 = quantile(r, .975))
    }
  
    r2_table <- data.frame(
      model = c("Binary (Bernoulli)", "Judged (Ordinal)", "Cosine (Beta)"),
      rbind(.r2(fit_bin), .r2(fit_ord), .r2(fit_cos_org))
    )
  
    # clean rounding
    r2_table$Estimate <- round(r2_table$Estimate, 3)
    r2_table$Q2.5     <- round(r2_table$Q2.5, 3)
    r2_table$Q97.5    <- round(r2_table$Q97.5, 3)
  
    # Save table to reuse later
    saveRDS(r2_table, .r2_rds)
    message("Saved new r2_table to ", .r2_rds)
  }
  

  ## ---- cleanup helpers (keep only model objects + r2_table + path vars) ----
  rm(list = c(".pri_bin",".pri_ord",".pri_wide",
              ".bin_rds",".ord_rds",".cos_org_rds", ".cos_com_rds",
              ".m_ord_cos_rds",".m_bin_cos_rds",".m_bin_jud_rds",".m_cos_jud_rds", ".r2_rds"))
}

4.3.1 Convergence

Rhat and Bulk ESS:

binary_diagnostics <- tibble(
  model = "binary",
  max_rhat = max(brms::rhat(fit_bin)),
  min_ess_bulk = min(brms::neff_ratio(fit_bin))
)
## Loading required namespace: rstan
ordinal_diagnostics <- tibble(
  model = "ordinal",
  max_rhat = max(brms::rhat(fit_ord)),
  min_ess_bulk = min(brms::neff_ratio(fit_ord))
)

cosine_diagnostics <- tibble(
  model = "cosine",
  max_rhat = max(brms::rhat(fit_cos_com)),
  min_ess_bulk = min(brms::neff_ratio(fit_cos_com))
)

bind_rows(binary_diagnostics, ordinal_diagnostics, cosine_diagnostics)

4.3.1.1 Cosine scale verification

# Extract stimulus posteriors from both models
stim_original <- fitted(fit_cos_org, 
                       newdata = data.frame(stimulus_concept = levels(df_brm$stimulus_concept)),
                       re_formula = ~(1|stimulus_concept))

stim_scaled <- fitted(fit_cos_com,
                     newdata = data.frame(stimulus_concept = levels(df_brm$stimulus_concept)),
                     re_formula = ~(1|stimulus_concept))

# Perfect rank preservation
cor(stim_original[,"Estimate"], stim_scaled[,"Estimate"], method = "spearman")
## [1] 0.9884316
# Should be as close to 1.0 as possible

Verify Rank Concordance

# Extract stimulus-level predictions from both
get_stim_preds <- function(fit, label) {
  nd <- data.frame(stimulus_concept = levels(df_brm$stimulus_concept))
  preds <- fitted(fit, newdata = nd, 
                  re_formula = ~(1|stimulus_concept), 
                  summary = TRUE)
  tibble(
    stimulus = nd$stimulus_concept,
    mean = preds[, "Estimate"],
    model = label
  )
}

stim_both <- bind_rows(
  get_stim_preds(fit_cos_org, "Original scale"),
  get_stim_preds(fit_cos_com, "Rescaled")
)

# Rank correlation (should be perfect)
stim_wide <- stim_both %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = mean)

cor(stim_wide$`Original scale`, stim_wide$`Rescaled`, method = "spearman")
## [1] 0.9884316
# Should be 1.0 - perfect rank preservation

# Visualize
ggplot(stim_wide, aes(x = `Original scale`, y = `Rescaled`)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Stimulus rankings preserved by rescaling")
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

4.3.2 Model summaries

# Binary model summary
summary(fit_bin)
##  Family: bernoulli 
##   Links: mu = logit 
## Formula: binary_guess ~ 1 + (1 | p | participant) + (1 | s | stimulus_concept) 
##    Data: df_brm (Number of observations: 25863) 
##   Draws: 4 chains, each with iter = 8000; warmup = 4000; thin = 1;
##          total post-warmup draws = 16000
## 
## Multilevel Hyperparameters:
## ~participant (Number of levels: 200) 
##               Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
## sd(Intercept)     1.50      0.11     1.29     1.73 1.00     4083     7530
## 
## ~stimulus_concept (Number of levels: 30) 
##               Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
## sd(Intercept)     3.48      0.67     2.43     5.02 1.00     4424     7598
## 
## Regression Coefficients:
##           Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
## Intercept    -7.11      0.73    -8.65    -5.75 1.00     3127     5494
## 
## Draws were sampled using sample(hmc). For each parameter, Bulk_ESS
## and Tail_ESS are effective sample size measures, and Rhat is the potential
## scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence, Rhat = 1).
binary_results <- tibble(
  parameter = c("Intercept", "SD_participant", "SD_stimulus"),
  mean = c(
    fixef(fit_bin)[1, "Estimate"],
    VarCorr(fit_bin)$participant$sd[1, "Estimate"],
    VarCorr(fit_bin)$stimulus_concept$sd[1, "Estimate"]
  ),
  ci_lower = c(
    fixef(fit_bin)[1, "Q2.5"],
    VarCorr(fit_bin)$participant$sd[1, "Q2.5"],
    VarCorr(fit_bin)$stimulus_concept$sd[1, "Q2.5"]
  ),
  ci_upper = c(
    fixef(fit_bin)[1, "Q97.5"],
    VarCorr(fit_bin)$participant$sd[1, "Q97.5"],
    VarCorr(fit_bin)$stimulus_concept$sd[1, "Q97.5"]
  )
)

binary_results

The Bayesian logistic regression model for binary accuracy (exact/near-exact matches) revealed that guessing success was very low overall. The population-level intercept of β = -7.11 (95% HDI [-8.65, -5.75]) on the logit scale corresponds to a baseline probability of approximately 0.08% (less than 1 in 1000) of producing an exact match when not accounting for specific stimuli or participants. This extremely negative intercept confirms that exact semantic matches were rare events. The model revealed substantial heterogeneity at both levels: participant-level variation (SD = 1.50, 95% HDI [1.29, 1.73]) indicated that some individuals were consistently better at guessing across all stimuli, while stimulus-level variation (SD = 3.48, 95% HDI [2.43, 5.02]) was even larger, demonstrating that certain concepts were dramatically more guessable than others. The large stimulus SD relative to the participant SD suggests that item characteristics (e.g., iconicity, semantic domain) played a more important role than individual differences in determining success.

ordinal_results

The cumulative logit model for ordinal judgments (0 = completely different, 1 = distantly related, 2 = similar, 3 = identical/near-identical) estimated three threshold parameters that define boundaries between adjacent response categories. The first threshold (between 0 and 1) was β = 3.90 (95% HDI [2.80, 5.03]), indicating a high barrier for responses to be considered even distantly related to targets. The second threshold (between 1 and 2) was β = 4.88 (95% HDI [3.78, 6.01]), and the third threshold (between 2 and 3) was β = 6.19 (95% HDI [5.09, 7.32]). These monotonically increasing thresholds show that each step up in similarity rating required increasingly strong evidence, with the gap between categories 2 and 3 (similar vs. identical) being particularly large. Participant-level variation was moderate (SD = 0.665, 95% HDI [0.580, 0.762]), suggesting relatively consistent rating behavior across individuals. However, stimulus-level variation was substantial (SD = 3.08, 95% HDI [2.28, 4.23]), confirming that some stimuli consistently elicited higher similarity ratings than others. The pattern mirrors the binary model: item characteristics mattered more than individual differences in determining semantic overlap between responses and targets.

cosine_results

The Beta regression model for cosine similarity scores (computational semantic overlap based on ConceptNet embeddings, scaled 0-1) estimated a population-level intercept of β = -0.534 (95% HDI [-0.863, -0.217]) on the logit scale. When back-transformed to the probability scale, this corresponds to a mean cosine similarity of approximately 0.37, indicating that participant responses were, on average, semantically closer to unrelated concepts than to the target meanings. The precision parameter φ = 2.75 describes the concentration of the Beta distribution, with higher values indicating less variance around the mean; this moderate value suggests considerable spread in cosine scores. Between-participant variation was relatively small (SD = 0.346, 95% HDI [0.311, 0.386]), indicating that participants showed similar levels of semantic distance from targets on average. In contrast, between-stimulus variation was substantially larger (SD = 0.878, 95% HDI [0.676, 1.16]), confirming that the semantic guessability of stimuli varied dramatically. As with the other two measures, this pattern demonstrates that the success or failure of semantic guessing was primarily driven by properties of the stimuli (e.g., which semantic domain they belonged to, their acoustic iconicity) rather than by individual participant abilities.

4.3.3 Compare outcome scales (pasted from claude just like that)

Binary model: P(Y = 1) → [0, 1] probability Cosine model: E(Y) → [0, 1] continuous Ordinal model: P(Y = 0,1,2,3) → How to map to [0,1]?

Ordinal to continuous mapping

# Helper function: extract expected value from ordinal model
get_ordinal_expected <- function(fit_ord, newdata) {
  # Get predicted probabilities for each category
  # fitted() for ordinal gives P(Y = k) for each k
  pred <- fitted(fit_ord, newdata = newdata, 
                 re_formula = ~(1|stimulus_concept),
                 summary = FALSE)  # Get all posterior draws
  
  # pred is array: draws × observations × categories
  # Dimensions: [n_draws, n_stimuli, 4 categories]
  
  # Compute expected value for each draw and stimulus
  # E(Y) = 0*P(Y=0) + 1*P(Y=1) + 2*P(Y=2) + 3*P(Y=3)
  expected_vals <- apply(pred, c(1, 2), function(probs) {
    sum(c(0, 1, 2, 3) * probs)
  })
  
   
  # Normalize to [0, 1]
  expected_vals_norm <- expected_vals / 3
  
  # Return summary statistics
  tibble(
    stimulus = newdata$stimulus_concept,
    Estimate = apply(expected_vals_norm, 2, mean),
    Q2.5 = apply(expected_vals_norm, 2, quantile, 0.025),
    Q97.5 = apply(expected_vals_norm, 2, quantile, 0.975)
    )
  }
  
  # Create newdata for all stimuli
  nd_stim <- data.frame(stimulus_concept = levels(df_brm$stimulus_concept))
  
  # Extract predictions from all three models
  stim_binary <- fitted(fit_bin, newdata = nd_stim,
                        re_formula = ~(1|stimulus_concept),
                        summary = TRUE) %>%
    as_tibble() %>%
    mutate(stimulus = nd_stim$stimulus_concept,
           measure = "Binary")
  
  stim_ordinal <- get_ordinal_expected(fit_ord, nd_stim) %>%
    mutate(measure = "Judged")
  
  stim_cosine <- fitted(fit_cos_com, newdata = nd_stim,
                        re_formula = ~(1|stimulus_concept),
                        summary = TRUE) %>%
    as_tibble() %>%
    mutate(stimulus = nd_stim$stimulus_concept,
           measure = "Cosine (rescaled)")
  
  # Combine all three
  all_measures <- bind_rows(
    stim_binary %>% select(stimulus, Estimate, Q2.5, Q97.5, measure),
    stim_ordinal %>% select(stimulus, Estimate, Q2.5, Q97.5, measure),
    stim_cosine %>% select(stimulus, Estimate, Q2.5, Q97.5, measure)
  ) %>%
    left_join(cats, by = c("stimulus" = "meaning"))

Across all three evaluation measures—binary accuracy, ordinal similarity judgments, and computational cosine similarity—a consistent pattern emerged: stimulus-level variation substantially exceeded participant-level variation. This indicates that the guessability of novel vocalizations and ape gestures was primarily determined by properties of the signals themselves (their iconicity, semantic domain, or other stimulus characteristics) rather than by individual cognitive differences among participants. The extremely low intercepts for binary accuracy and the below-midpoint intercept for cosine similarity both confirm that, in absolute terms, semantic guessing success was limited when the response space was unrestricted, even though relative differences between stimuli were substantial and systematic.

Critical Code Block: Getting Ordinal Expected Values If the above get_ordinal_expected() function doesn’t work with your brms version, here’s a more robust alternative:

# Alternative method using posterior_predict
get_ordinal_expected_v2 <- function(fit_ord, newdata) {
  # Get posterior predicted categories for each draw
  pred_cats <- posterior_predict(fit_ord, 
                                 newdata = newdata,
                                 re_formula = ~(1|stimulus_concept))
  
  # pred_cats is matrix: draws × observations
  # Values are 0, 1, 2, or 3
  
  # Convert categories to [0,1] scale
  pred_norm <- pred_cats / 3
  
  # Summarize across draws
  tibble(
    stimulus = newdata$stimulus_concept,
    Estimate = apply(pred_norm, 2, mean),
    Q2.5 = apply(pred_norm, 2, quantile, 0.025),
    Q97.5 = apply(pred_norm, 2, quantile, 0.975)
  )
}

# Test both methods and compare
stim_ord_v1 <- get_ordinal_expected(fit_ord, nd_stim)
stim_ord_v2 <- get_ordinal_expected_v2(fit_ord, nd_stim)

# Should be highly correlated (might differ slightly)
